title: Intro to Full Stack Dev
summary: A concepts-only lesson on how a web app works end to end: the front-end, back-end, database and infrastructure layers, and how a request travels from the browser to a server and back (IP, TCP, DNS, HTTP, AJAX, JSON).
goal: Trace a user action from the screen to the database and back, naming the HTTP method and status code at each step.
required: Part I: Knowledge Check 1 – Intro to Full Stack (team quiz, FS-Knowledge-Check-1)
Part II: Knowledge Check 2 – Full Stack Development Breakdown (team quiz, fs-knowledge-check-2)

steps.title: Read Full Stack Workflow
steps.detail: Read the lecture's four layers (front-end, back-end, database, infrastructure) and its "You Open Instagram" walkthrough. The point is a mental model, not code.
steps.doneWhen: You can say in one sentence what each of the four layers is responsible for.

steps.title: Learn the web vocabulary
steps.detail: IP is WHERE a server is, TCP is HOW the bytes get there reliably, HTTP is WHAT the message says, and AJAX lets a page send requests without reloading. Knowledge Check 1 also covers DNS and JSON. Write one line on each in a topic note such as notes/topics/how-the-web-works.md.
steps.doneWhen: Your note explains IP, TCP, DNS, HTTP, AJAX and JSON in your own words.

steps.title: Take Knowledge Check 1 with your team
steps.detail: Open assignments/week-01/FS-Knowledge-Check-1 in VS Code, right-click index.html → Open with Live Server. After each question, discuss why the answer is right or wrong. progress.md shows this done; retake it alone to see what stuck.
steps.doneWhen: You finished the quiz and can explain the reasoning behind any answer you missed.

steps.title: Read Full Stack Breakdown
steps.detail: This lecture covers the HTTP conversation, front-end components that depend on data, and the back-end's job of validating and serializing data. Keep its "Rinse and Repeat" cycle in mind: request, response, UI update.
steps.doneWhen: You can explain why HTTP is called stateless and what serialization means.

steps.title: Map CRUD to HTTP methods and status codes
steps.detail: Make a small table in your topic note: each CRUD action, its HTTP method, and the status codes you'd expect. You'll use this exact mapping in AI-7, when you send requests to Supabase from Postman.
steps.code:
Create → POST
Read   → GET
Update → PUT / PATCH
Delete → DELETE
steps.doneWhen: Your table lists all four actions plus what 2xx, 4xx and 5xx codes mean.

steps.title: Take Knowledge Check 2 with your team
steps.detail: Same Live Server routine in assignments/week-01/fs-knowledge-check-2. It covers HTTP methods and status codes, CRUD, serialization, and front-end vs back-end jobs.
steps.doneWhen: Quiz finished, and you discussed every answer you got wrong.

steps.title: Diagram one request in your Netflix clone
steps.detail: The lesson's assignments are conceptual: you should be able to diagram a request flow. Pick one action in Myflix (assignments/week-02/netflix), such as adding a title to My List, and draw it through all the layers in TLDraw or a Mermaid diagram in your notes.
steps.doneWhen: Your diagram shows browser → request (method) → Supabase → table → response (status code) → UI update.

concepts.meaning: Understanding every layer of an app (UI, server logic, data and hosting) and how they talk to each other.
The part users see and click, running in the browser.
The server code that applies business rules, validates data and talks to the database.
IP finds where a server is; TCP delivers the data there reliably and in order.
The internet's phone book: it turns a name like netflix.com into an IP address.
The format for web requests and responses; it's stateless, so every request stands on its own.
Sending a request from JavaScript in the background so the page updates without a full reload.
A text format for data ({"key": "value"}) that front-ends and back-ends send to each other.
Create, Read, Update, Delete: the four things almost every app does with data.
The number in a response that tells you what happened: 2xx worked, 4xx your request was wrong, 5xx the server broke.
Turning data into a format like JSON so it can travel over the network.
